title: How Whiskey Runners Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss whiskey running and moonshining in the rural South, tracing how the Great Depression, Prohibition, and dry counties fueled bootlegging. They cover souped-up cars, evasion tactics like Clay Call's brake-light switches and Junior Johnson's Bootleggers turn, the revenuers (federal Alcohol Tax Unit agents) who chased them, and how the bootlegging culture gave rise to dirt track racing and NASCAR, including the discovery of drafting. They also mention the film Lawless, related episodes, a Comic Con live show and trivia night announcement, and a listener email about a shark attack survivor.

entities.name: The Wettest County in the World

segments.title: Opening banter and related episodes
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about Dinosaurs and past episodes, mention the earlier moonshine, Prohibition, and rehab episodes, and introduce the topic of moonshining and bootlegging.

segments.title: NASCAR's bootlegging roots
segments.summary: The hosts say NASCAR was founded by moonshiners and bootleggers, with Junior Johnson as an example. Wilkes County, North Carolina is named as a bootlegging hotbed and NASCAR's home region.

segments.title: Depression, Prohibition, and dry counties
segments.summary: The South's economy collapsed during the Great Depression as mills closed and farming declined, while Prohibition and dry counties created demand for illegal liquor. Bootleggers kept selling to dry counties, and avoiding taxes was also a motive, tracing back to the Whiskey Rebellion.

segments.title: Young drivers and souped-up cars
segments.summary: Teenagers in farm families often ran liquor, with the hosts describing how young drivers became skilled. The hosts describe modified cars, such as a Ford with a Cadillac ambulance engine, and switching engines between makes.

segments.title: Revenuers and evasion tactics
segments.summary: Federal revenue agents, including John Carter, chased runners who knew the back roads and their modified cars. Clay Call's brake and tail light cut-off switches, false-bottom trunks, and heavy-duty shocks helped them evade police. Thunder Road in North Georgia was dangerous to drive.

segments.title: Bootleggers turn and drafting
segments.summary: Junior Johnson is credited with the Bootleggers turn maneuver. He also discovered drafting by accident during a 1960 race, which led to the technique being named and used in racing.

segments.title: Junior Johnson's arrest, later bootlegging, and the chicken farming shift
segments.summary: Junior Johnson was caught at his father's still by John Carter and served prison time. Bootleggers were reportedly so honest they waited for the prison bus. Clay Call continued bootlegging into the 1980s, and chicken processing plants led many distillers to switch careers.

segments.title: Dirt tracks and the shift to stock car racing
segments.summary: Rural Southerners built dirt tracks for entertainment, and bootleggers preferred dirt roads. Organized stock car racing then developed, with rules limiting modifications and emphasizing driver skill and fan identification with car brands.

segments.title: Bootlegging films
segments.summary: The hosts mention movies about moonshine and bootlegging, including Lawless, based on The Wettest County in the World, and several other films.

segments.title: Live show and trivia announcement
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce a live show at Comic Con in New York and a trivia night at the Cutting Room on October 12.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode with contact information for listener mail and social media.
